title: Convenience store checkout
setting: You've picked up a bento and a drink at a Lawson. You're at the till.

options.english: (Nod slightly and put your items on the counter.)
options.feedback: Correct. いらっしゃいませ is a greeting *to* a customer and expects no verbal reply at all.
Perfectly fine — a little more than needed, and never unwelcome.
This is the giveaway. You've just welcomed the shop assistant into their own shop. It's only ever said staff-to-customer.

n2.speaker: staff
n2.english: Shall I heat up the bento?
n2.audioHint: おべんとう、あたためますか

options.feedback: Yes please. お願いします on its own is a complete, polite answer to any offer.
A soft no. 大丈夫です declines without a blunt いいえ.
Honest and it works — they'll mime the microwave. But 温めますか is one of the five sentences you'll hear most in Japan, so it's worth over-learning.

n3.speaker: staff
n3.audioHint: ふくろはごりようですか

options.feedback: Clear and complete. Bags are chargeable, so this question is now unavoidable.
Yes to a bag, and you'll be charged a few yen for it.
はい is understood as 'yes, a bag please' — but bare はい to an either/or question is a common way to accidentally agree to the wrong thing.

n4.speaker: staff
n4.japanese: 五百八十円になります。

furigana.r: ごひゃくはちじゅうえん

n4.audioHint: ごひゃくはちじゅうえんになります

options.feedback: Card works at every convenience store in the country. Tap it on the reader yourself when prompted.
Exact change, handed to the tray rather than the hand. There's usually a small tray on the counter for this.
They just told you the price. Asking again reads as 'I didn't catch that' — which is fine, but もう一度お願いします says it far more clearly.

n5.speaker: staff
n5.japanese: ありがとうございました。またお越しくださいませ。

furigana.b: ありがとうございました。またお

n5.audioHint: ありがとうございました。またおこしくださいませ

options.feedback: The transaction is finished, so the past form is exactly right.
'You're welcome' to the person who just served you inverts the roles. A simple thanks, or nothing at all, is what's expected.

end.speaker: narration
end.english: Done. That exchange is near-identical at every convenience store in Japan — get it fluent once and it's solved for the whole trip.
